messages.author: 74c21b66ea98edf2
messages.subject: Obsever Experience
parts:
Hello All,

I was interested to know if any of you have used observer experience as a covariate in your distance model. Particularly, I am interested in how you chose to quantify experience and whether this was a useful covariate or not.

We fly helicopter-based line transect surveys for quail and employ 3 observers plus the pilot. We have noticed that in some surveys with multiple new observers (2 or more) that our detection probability is much lower closer to the transect line (0-10m). This problem doesn't seem to appear nearly ever with experienced observers.

Any information on this subject is most appreciated regardless of survey type or species.

Thanks,

John Edwards


John Edwards
Ph.D. Research Assistant

messages.author: 73b62f7cf4931a76
messages.subject: Re: Obsever Experience
parts:
We looked at this question using a 20-yr, large scale riparian bird community monitoring project with multiple observers with various levels of experience.  Using #of field seasons with the project there was a modest effect on overall densities (due to differences in mean distances), more of an effect on diversity metrics from total #field seasons (from applications that were kept on file).  But there were very large differences between even equally experiences observers.  Ultimately we felt it all had to come out in the wash through good study design & implementation.  For example, we used the analysis argue for shifting to a spatially balanced design (did not happen), got serious about randomly rotating observers, and got very serious about our training program (or programme, as this is an international listserv...).  There is systematic variance you can control for, model the effects of, or assume away.  But we never did publish anything on it.

Cheers -

Russ Norvell
Avian Conservation Program Coordinator
Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

John

Another example paper using observer experience is

@article{Borchers2006,
author = {Borchers, D. L. and Laake, J. L. and Southwell, C. and
Paxton, C. G. M.},
title = {Accommodating unmodeled heterogeneity in double-observer
distance sampling surveys},
journal = {Biometrics},
year = {2006},
volume = {62},
pages = {372--378}
}

Here is the paragraph from the Methods section describing the covariates
they employed in their detection function modelling

Variables recorded in addition to distance were: group size (a factor
with three levels), “platform” (front or back seat), whether the
observer was on the left or right of the aircraft, the observer
identity, observer experience (total hours surveying on the survey),
time since start of flight, time on-effort since last rest, visibility
category (a factor with three levels), presence/absence of shadows, and
ice cover (a factor with
three levels).

These data were also distributed during the Advanced distance sampling
workshop as "CrabbieMCDSExercise" and "CrabbieMRDSExercise".

messages.author: 51849154d78f6349
messages.subject: RE: Obsever Experience
parts:
Hello all

Another example in :
Defos du Rau, P., Bourgeois, K., Thévenet, M., Ruffino, L., Dromzée, S., Ouni, R., ... & Faggio, G. (2015). Reassessment of the size of the Scopoli's Shearwater population at its main breeding site resulted in a tenfold increase: implications for the species conservation. Journal of Ornithology, 156(4), 877-892.

Here are the descriptions of two covariates we used that might be of interest to you (although I think the first one is probably too basic and the second one required a bit of field trial):

Observer experience (OE)
absence of experience was rated 1; experience in bird survey was rated 2; experience in seabird survey was rated 3

Observer detection skills (OD)
Observer-specific detection probability as calculated from one test transect of 53 nests that was surveyed by all observers. Individual detection skills were computed as the ratio of the number of detected nests to the total number of nests (53)

None of them was influent, possibly because in our relatively lengthy field work, even inexperienced observers had plenty of time to gain an accurate search image.
Best
Pierre
